newsitem.title: UK: Police treating IRA bomb claim as "real threat".
newsitem.headline: Police treating IRA bomb claim as "real threat".

text.p: Northern Ireland police said on Saturday they were treating seriously an IRA claim that its guerrillas had abandoned a defused landmine in a Catholic area of west Belfast.

It was the Irish Republican Army's first reported hostile action in the province since the Labour Party scored a landslide victory in a British general election on May 1 and resumed ties with the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing that had been abandoned by the previous Conservative government.

A caller using an Irish Republican Army identity codeword told a local radio station that its "engineers" had defused the device before dumping it. According to the caller, the landmine was abandoned "because of civilian activity in the area".
Two hours after the alarm was raised, police had still not moved into the area where the device was said to have been dumped, security sources said.
They said they did not know whether the operation was a hoax but vowed to tread warily in case the guerrillas were trying to lure them into a trap.

Britain ended contacts with Sinn Fein in February 1996 when the IRA scrapped a 17-month ceasefire by setting off a huge bomb in the Docklands commercial and residential area of London's East End, killing two people and causing hundreds of millions of dollars worth of property damage.
Shortly after winning power at the beginning of May, Prime Minister Tony Blair allowed the resumption of talks between government officials and the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing.
But Blair made clear the talks could only take place if the IRA refrained from using violence. Two rounds of talks have been held in the past 10 days and another is due soon.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, during a brief official visit to Britain on Thursday, urged the IRA to lay down its arms and said it had to compromise in order to join multi-party peace talks aimed at ending three decades of bloody conflict over the future of the British-controlled province.

The IRA has often set off explosive devices in Catholic areas to catch British security patrols. Police superintendent Ian Williamson said the IRA had carried out surveillance exercises on British forces patrols recently.

"This might be a Sinn Fein/IRA propaganda exercise. However bearing in mind that an authenticated codeword was used to a local radio station, it has to be treated as a very real terrorist threat," Williamson said in a statement.

"While it does appear to some that there has been a recent lull in violence, terrorist activity on the ground in this area has remained at a significant level, particularly in regard to targetting of security forces' personnel and patrols."
The IRA is fighting to end Britain's rule over the province. The majority Protestants support Union with Britain but the minority Roman Catholics want an all-Ireland state.
The last IRA attack in the province was on April 10 when a sniper seriously wounded a policewoman guarding a courthouse in the city of Londonderry.

Tension has been high for many months amid a threat of IRA violence and sporadic attacks by their foes in banned Protestant "Loyalist" groups who have shot dead two Catholics this year and injured several others gun and bomb attacks.

Multi-party talks on the province are due to take place on Tuesday in Belfast after a three-month adjournment, chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchell. Britain and Ireland say that the only way Sinn Fein will be admitted is if the IRA abandons violence.
